BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of Histology:
What Histology Is & How a Slide Is Made

Histology is the study of tissues under the microscope — the bridge between naked-eye anatomy and cell biology. Almost every slide you meet is a thin, stained slice of tissue on glass, and knowing how it was made explains most of what you see (and most artefacts).

A biopsy becomes a slide through a fixed pipeline — each step preserves structure and makes cells visible.
1
Fixation10% neutral-buffered formalin: cross-links proteins, halts autolysis & decay, hardens tissue
↓
2
Dehydration & clearingGraded alcohols remove water; xylene clears the alcohol so wax can infiltrate
↓
3
EmbeddingTissue set in a paraffin wax block for support
↓
4
MicrotomyCut into 3–5 µm sections and floated onto a slide
↓
5
Rehydrate, stain, mountWax removed, tissue rehydrated, stained (usually H&E), sealed under a coverslip
Frozen section is the fast route — tissue is snap-frozen and cut on a cryostat, skipping wax. It gives a diagnosis in minutes (vs ~24 h for routine wax processing — intra-operative margin assessment) and is the main way to preserve lipids and many enzymes, at the cost of poorer morphology.
H&E — The Workhorse Stain ⭐

Haematoxylin & Eosin stains >95% of routine slides. Two dyes of opposite charge partition the tissue by chemistry:

🔬 Image slot — a labelled H&E section showing blue nuclei & pink cytoplasm
🔵 Haematoxylin → basophilic (blue–purple)
  • A basic dye binding acidic (negatively charged) structures
  • Nuclei / chromatin & nucleoli (DNA)
  • Rough ER & ribosomes (RNA) → blue cytoplasm in secretory cells
  • Cartilage matrix, calcium, some mucins
🔴 Eosin → eosinophilic / acidophilic (pink)
  • An acidic dye binding basic (positively charged) proteins
  • Cytoplasm (most proteins), collagen, muscle
  • Red blood cells (brilliant pink), keratin
  • Most extracellular matrix
Read the colours as chemistry: "blue = nucleic-acid–rich", so a cell with blue cytoplasm is busy making protein (plasma cell, pancreatic acinar cell); "pink = protein-rich cytoplasm/matrix".
Watch the double-negative: a basic dye (haematoxylin) binds acidic structures, and an acidic dye (eosin) binds basic ones — dye and target always have opposite chemistry.

Three that win exam questions: Congo red → amyloid (apple-green birefringence) · Ziehl–Neelsen → TB · PAS → fungi & basement membrane.
Immunohistochemistry (IHC)

Uses labelled antibodies to detect specific antigens — it answers "what kind of cell is this?", above all when classifying a tumour of uncertain origin.

Cytokeratins (CK) → epithelial → carcinoma
Vimentin → mesenchymal (sarcoma) — non-specific
CD45 (LCA) → leucocytes → lymphoma
S100 → melanoma (sensitive), nerve, cartilage; HMB-45 / Melan-A = specific for melanoma
Ki-67 → proliferation index (correlates with grade; defines grade in neuroendocrine tumours)
ER / PR / HER2 → breast cancer, guides therapy
IHC turns morphology into a lineage diagnosis and increasingly a treatment decision (HER2-positive breast cancer → trastuzumab).
How to Read a Slide — A Systematic Approach ⭐

Never start on high power. Zoom out to orient, then in to identify.

🔬 Image slot — same field at low vs high power to show the zoom-out-then-in approach
1
Low power — orientation & architectureIs there a capsule? Overall pattern — layered tube (GI), lobules (gland/liver), follicles (thyroid/lymph node), tubules (kidney/testis)? First guess at the organ.
↓
2
Medium power — functional unitFind the repeating unit: villus + crypt, glomerulus + tubules, seminiferous tubule, gastric gland. Identify the lining epithelium.
↓
3
High power — cells & specialisationsName the cell types; read the nuclei; spot cilia, brush border, striations, secretory granules, keratin.
The four questions that name most tissue
Epithelium or connective tissue? Cells packed with little matrix vs sparse cells in abundant matrix.
Simple or stratified? One layer (absorb/secrete) vs many (protect).
Cell shape? Squamous, cuboidal or columnar → names the epithelium.
Surface specialisation? Cilia (airway), brush border (gut/kidney), keratin (skin).
Microscopy & Resolution
🔬 Light microscope
  • Total magnification = objective × eyepiece (40× × 10× = 400×)
  • Useful to ~1000×; resolution ~0.2 µm (limited by the wavelength of light)
  • Shows cells, nuclei, tissue architecture
⚛️ Electron microscope
  • TEM → ultrastructure: organelles, basement membrane, cell junctions, cilia axoneme (9+2)
  • SEM → 3-D surface
  • Needs glutaraldehyde + osmium tetroxide fixation, resin embedding & ultrathin sections
  • Resolution to ~0.2 nm (electrons have a far shorter wavelength)
When you NEED EM: a filtration-barrier lesion on renal biopsy (podocyte foot processes, GBM), primary ciliary dyskinesia (absent dynein arms), and junctions/granules too small for light microscopy.
Artefacts — Don't Call Them Pathology
  • Folds & tears — from cutting/floating
  • Knife (chatter) marks — parallel lines from a nicked blade
  • Shrinkage clefts — white spaces around cells
  • Air bubbles under the coverslip
  • Formalin pigment — brown/black granules
  • Freezing artefact — ice-crystal holes
If a "lesion" is perfectly straight, perfectly round, or sits partly off the tissue, suspect an artefact — not disease.
Clinical Correlate — From Biopsy to Diagnosis

Histology is the diagnosis in much of medicine — a cancer is defined by what the pathologist sees.

Routine biopsy
Formalin → wax → H&E → report on cell type, grade, margins, invasion.
Frozen section
Minutes, intra-operative — "is this tumour?", "are the margins clear?"
Special stains
Congo red → amyloid; ZN → TB; PAS-D → fungi / storage; Perls' → iron.
IHC / molecular
Tumour lineage & therapy targets (ER/PR/HER2, Ki-67).
⭐ Exam Pearls
Basophilic = blue (nuclei, RER/ribosomes, DNA/RNA); eosinophilic = pink (cytoplasmic protein, collagen, muscle, RBC).
Routine fixative = 10% neutral-buffered formalin; sections cut at 3–5 µm.
Lipids need frozen sections (Oil Red O / Sudan) — the solvents (alcohols/xylene) in processing dissolve fat.
Congo red + apple-green birefringence = amyloid.
PAS → glycogen, basement membrane, fungi; PAS-diastase removes glycogen to confirm it.
Masson's trichrome grades fibrosis (collagen blue/green).
Light microscopy resolution ~0.2 µm; use EM for basement membrane, cilia & junctions.
Always read low power first — architecture before cytology.
BASIC TISSUES__Epithelium (types, juncti:
Overview — What Epithelium Is

Epithelium is a sheet of tightly packed cells that covers surfaces, lines cavities and tubes, and forms glands. It derives from all three germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm).

Defining features
  • Cellular — packed cells, minimal matrix (opposite of connective tissue)
  • Avascular — fed by diffusion from underlying connective tissue
  • Rests on a basement membrane
  • Polarised (apical / lateral / basal domains)
  • Held together by cell junctions; high regenerative capacity
Functions
  • Protection (skin)
  • Absorption (gut, kidney)
  • Secretion (glands)
  • Filtration (glomerulus)
  • Sensation & lubrication
How It's Classified & Recognised ⭐

Name an epithelium in two steps: (1) number of layers × (2) shape of the surface cell.

By layers
  • Simple — one layer
  • Stratified — many layers
  • Pseudostratified — one layer but nuclei at different heights, so it looks layered (all cells touch the BM)
By surface-cell shape
  • Squamous — flat
  • Cuboidal — cube
  • Columnar — tall
  • Special: transitional (urothelium)
Reading a slide: count the layers (simple vs stratified), judge the apical cell shape, then look for surface specialisations (cilia, brush border, keratin). For stratified epithelium, the surface layer names it.
The Epithelial Types

Stratified squamous — non-keratinisedProtection (moist)Oral cavity, oesophagus, vagina, anal canal
Transitional (urothelium)Stretch + impermeable barrierBladder, ureters, renal pelvis — dome-shaped umbrella cells that flatten when full
Cell Junctions (apical → basal)
JunctionMade ofJob
Tight junction (zonula occludens)Claudins/occludinsSeals the gap — blocks paracellular leak & maintains polarity
Adherens junction (zonula adherens)Cadherins → actin beltMechanical adhesion; shapes the epithelium

The apical junctional complex = tight junction + adherens junction + desmosome (e.g. between enterocytes) — the terminal bar seen on light microscopy. Zonula = continuous belt (tight/adherens); macula = spot (desmosome); gap junctions lie separately along the lateral membrane.
Surface Specialisations (Apical & Basal)
Microvilli (brush border)
Actin-cored finger-like projections that increase surface area for absorption — gut, kidney PCT.
Cilia
Motile (9+2 axoneme, dynein) — sweep mucus/ova along the respiratory tract & uterine tube.
Stereocilia
Long, non-motile microvilli — epididymis and cochlear hair cells.
Keratin
Tough, waterproofing surface layer of the epidermis.
Basolateral infoldings
Deep basal membrane folds packed with mitochondria — power ion/water transport; give the “striations” of kidney tubules & salivary striated ducts.
Basement Membrane & Polarity
Basement membrane
  • Basal lamina (lamina lucida + densa: type IV collagen + laminin, made by epithelium) + reticular lamina (type III, from CT)
  • Attaches epithelium to CT, guides regeneration, and filters (glomerulus)
  • PAS-positive
  • Disease links: Alport (mutant type IV collagen → GBM splitting, haematuria, deafness); Goodpasture (anti–type IV collagen antibodies); diabetic BM thickening
Polarity — three domains
  • Apical — faces the lumen/surface (microvilli, cilia)
  • Lateral — carries the cell junctions
  • Basal — hemidesmosomes onto the basement membrane
Glands — Epithelium That Secretes
Exocrine vs endocrine
  • Exocrine — secrete via ducts onto a surface (sweat, pancreas)
  • Endocrine — ductless, secrete hormones into blood (thyroid, islets)
  • A goblet cell is a unicellular exocrine gland (mucus)
Mode of exocrine secretion
  • Merocrine/eccrine — exocytosis, cell intact (most; sweat, pancreas)
  • Apocrine — apical cytoplasm pinched off (mammary, some sweat)
  • Holocrine — whole cell disintegrates (sebaceous)
Gland architecture: simple (unbranched duct) vs compound (branched) × tubular / acinar / tubuloacinar secretory unit — sweat = simple coiled tubular; sebaceous = simple branched acinar; salivary/pancreas = compound tubuloacinar.
Serous glands make a watery, protein-rich secretion (pancreas, parotid); mucous glands make viscous mucin (goblet cells, sublingual); many are mixed.
Stains & Ultrastructure
  • H&E — routine identification
  • PAS — basement membrane, goblet-cell mucin & brush border (magenta)
  • Cytokeratin (IHC) — marks epithelial cells → identifies a carcinoma
  • EM — needed to see cilia (9+2), microvilli cores and junction ultrastructure
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Metaplasia
Reversible change of one epithelium to another — Barrett's (oesophageal squamous→columnar); ciliated→squamous in smokers.
Dysplasia → carcinoma
Disordered growth → carcinoma in situ → invasive carcinoma (the commonest cancers).
Carcinoma subtypes
SCC (squamous), adenocarcinoma (glandular), urothelial/transitional (bladder) — all cytokeratin-positive.
Primary ciliary dyskinesia
Defective ciliary dynein → bronchiectasis, infertility, situs inversus (Kartagener).
Pemphigus vulgaris
Autoantibodies vs desmoglein (desmosomes) → intra-epidermal (flaccid) blisters.
Bullous pemphigoid
Autoantibodies vs hemidesmosome proteins (BP180/BP230) → sub-epidermal tense blisters (elderly).
Coeliac disease
Immune damage to absorptive enterocytes → villous atrophy, malabsorption.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Pemphigus = desmosome / intra-epidermal (flaccid); pemphigoid = hemidesmosome / sub-epidermal (tense).
Name it by layers × surface-cell shape; for stratified, the surface layer names it.
Pseudostratified = one layer that looks layered (all cells touch the BM) — classically respiratory (ciliated + goblet).
Simple squamous: endothelium (vessels) & mesothelium (serosa), alveoli, glomerulus.
Transitional/urothelium = bladder/ureter (umbrella cells, stretch).
Junctions: tight (seal) → adherens (actin) → desmosome (keratin, strength) → gap (communication) → hemidesmosome (to BM).
Microvilli = absorption (brush border); cilia = 9+2, move mucus; keratin = protection.
Glands: sebaceous = holocrine; mammary/some sweat = apocrine; most = merocrine; goblet cell = unicellular gland.
Carcinoma = malignant epithelium, cytokeratin-positive; Barrett's = metaplasia; Pemphigus = desmosome antibodies.
Basement membrane is PAS-positive (type IV collagen + laminin).
BASIC TISSUES__Connective Tissue (loose,:
Overview — The Universal Plan

Connective tissue (CT) is the most abundant and diverse tissue — it connects, supports, binds and protects. It arises from embryonic mesenchyme.

The defining feature: unlike epithelium (packed cells, scant matrix), CT is sparse cells in an abundant extracellular matrix. CT = cells + matrix, and matrix = fibres + ground substance.
Classification
CT proper
  • Loose (areolar), adipose, reticular
  • Dense regular & dense irregular
Specialised CT
  • Cartilage, bone, blood — see their own notes
  • Adipose & reticular tissue (below)
The Cells — Resident vs Wandering
🔬 Image slot — loose areolar spread showing fibroblasts, collagen & elastic fibres
CellOriginRole & appearance
Fibroblast (fibrocyte = resting)MesenchymeCommonest CT cell; spindle-shaped; secretes fibres & ground substance
AdipocyteMesenchymeFat storage; signet-ring — a single lipid droplet pushes the nucleus to the rim
MacrophageBlood monocytePhagocytosis + antigen presentation (mononuclear phagocyte system)
Mast cellBone marrowGranules of histamine + heparin; drives allergy/inflammation; metachromatic with toluidine blue
Plasma cell (wandering)B lymphocyteSecretes antibodies; clock-face/cartwheel nucleus, basophilic cytoplasm, pale perinuclear hof
Leukocytes (wandering)BloodNeutrophils, eosinophils, lymphocytes, monocytes migrate in during inflammation
Resident (fixed) cells live in the CT (fibroblast, adipocyte, macrophage, mast cell, stem cells). Wandering (transient) cells arrive from blood (plasma cells, leukocytes).
The Fibres
Collagen (mostly type I)
The most abundant protein in the body; strong, tensile; eosinophilic (pink) wavy bundles on H&E.
Reticular (type III collagen)
Fine branching mesh; the framework/stroma of liver, lymph node & marrow; invisible on H&E — shown black by silver stains.
Elastic (elastin + fibrillin)
Stretch & recoil; large arteries, some ligaments; needs an elastic stain (Verhoeff/orcein) to see.
Ground Substance
  • An amorphous, hydrated gel filling the space between cells and fibres
  • GAGs (hyaluronic acid, chondroitin/dermatan/keratan sulfate), proteoglycans, and adhesive glycoproteins (fibronectin, laminin) + tissue fluid
  • Resists compression, and is the medium for diffusion of nutrients/wastes between capillaries and cells
Excess tissue fluid in the ground substance = oedema.
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
  • Sparse cells in abundant pink matrix — the opposite of epithelium
  • Spindle-shaped fibroblast nuclei lying along pink collagen bundles
  • Loose (areolar) — loosely woven fibres with obvious spaces & many cell types
  • Dense regular — tightly packed parallel wavy pink bundles (tendon) with fibroblasts squeezed between
  • Adipose — empty-looking signet-ring cells (fat dissolved in processing)
Types of Connective Tissue
🔬 Image slot — dense regular tendon & adipose tissue for comparison
TypeStructureWhere / function
Loose (areolar)Loosely arranged fibres (all types), many cells, abundant ground substanceThe "packing material" — lamina propria under epithelia, around vessels/nerves; general support
Dense regularParallel collagen bundles; fibroblasts in rows betweenTendons, ligaments, aponeuroses — tensile strength in one direction
Dense irregularCollagen bundles in random directionsDermis, organ capsules, submucosa, periosteum — resists tension from all directions
Reticular tissueNetwork of reticular (type III) fibres + reticular cellsStroma of lymphoid organs & bone marrow
Elastic tissueDense elastic fibresLarge arteries, ligamenta flava, vocal ligament
Adipose tissue — white vs brown
White adipose
  • Unilocular — one large droplet, nucleus at the rim (signet-ring)
  • Energy store, insulation, cushioning; endocrine (leptin, adiponectin)
Brown adipose
  • Multilocular — many droplets, central nucleus, many mitochondria
  • Thermogenesis via UCP1; prominent in neonates
Stains & Ultrastructure
  • H&E — collagen pink; cells with blue nuclei
  • Masson's trichrome — collagen blue/green (grades fibrosis)
  • Reticulin (silver) — reticular fibres black (organ frameworks)
  • Elastic (Verhoeff / orcein) — elastic fibres black/brown
  • Toluidine blue — mast cells (metachromasia)
  • Fat dissolves in processing, so adipocytes look empty — use Oil Red O on frozen tissue to see lipid
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Ehlers–Danlos
Defective collagen → hypermobile joints, stretchy fragile skin, easy bruising.
Marfan syndrome
FBN1 (fibrillin) defect → weak elastic tissue → aortic aneurysm/dissection, lens dislocation.
Scurvy
Vitamin C deficiency → failed collagen cross-linking → poor wound healing, bleeding gums.
Mast-cell degranulation
Type I hypersensitivity → histamine release → allergy/anaphylaxis.
Multiple myeloma
Malignant plasma cells → excess monoclonal antibody.
Keloid / fibrosis
Excess collagen deposition — keloid scar; organ fibrosis.
⭐ Exam Pearls
CT = cells + matrix; matrix = fibres + ground substance; derived from mesenchyme.
Fibroblast = commonest cell, makes the matrix.
Fibres: collagen I (strength, pink), reticular = collagen III (silver-stained frameworks), elastic (recoil, needs elastic stain).
Dense regular = tendons/ligaments (parallel); dense irregular = dermis/capsules (random).
Loose/areolar = the general-purpose packing tissue (lamina propria).
White fat = unilocular (signet-ring, storage); brown fat = multilocular (UCP1 thermogenesis, neonates).
Plasma cell = clock-face nucleus + perinuclear hof; mast cell = toluidine-blue metachromasia.
Clinical: Ehlers–Danlos/scurvy = collagen; Marfan = fibrillin/elastic.
BASIC TISSUES__Blood & Haemopoiesis (cel:
Overview — Blood as a Fluid Connective Tissue

Blood is a specialised connective tissue in which the cells (formed elements) are suspended in a fluid matrix, plasma — the only connective tissue whose matrix is liquid.

Formed elements (~45%)
  • Red cells (erythrocytes) — the vast majority
  • White cells (leukocytes)
  • Platelets (thrombocytes)
Plasma (~55%)
  • ~90% water + proteins (albumin, globulins, fibrinogen), electrolytes, nutrients, wastes
  • Serum = plasma minus clotting factors
Spun blood separates into packed red cells (bottom), a thin buffy coat of white cells + platelets (middle), and plasma (top). The red-cell fraction = the haematocrit.
Functions
Transport — O₂/CO₂, nutrients, hormones, waste
Defence — immunity (leukocytes, antibodies)
Haemostasis — clotting (platelets, fibrinogen)
Homeostasis — pH buffering, thermoregulation
The Blood Film — How It's Prepared & Read ⭐

A drop of blood is smeared and stained with a Romanowsky stain (Giemsa, Wright or Leishman) — a combination of acidic eosin (stains basic structures pink/red) and basic methylene blue (stains acidic structures blue/purple).

🔬 Image slot — a stained peripheral blood film (monolayer at the feathered edge)
  • Examine the feathered edge, where cells lie in a single layer (a monolayer)
  • A normal RBC is ~7–8 µm — use it as a built-in ruler to size white cells and judge red-cell size
Red Blood Cells (Erythrocytes)
🔬 Image slot — red cells showing biconcave discs with central pallor
Appearance
  • Biconcave disc, ~7–8 µm
  • Anucleate, no organelles — packed with haemoglobin
  • Eosinophilic (pink) with a pale central pallor (~⅓ of the diameter)
Structure → function
  • Biconcave shape → high surface-area:volume for gas exchange + deformability through capillaries
  • No nucleus/organelles → maximum room for Hb, but cannot repair → lifespan ~120 days
  • Removed by splenic & hepatic macrophages
Reticulocyte = a young red cell still containing residual ribosomal RNA. It looks faintly blue (polychromasia) on a routine film; a supravital stain (new methylene blue) shows its reticular network. A high count signals brisk marrow output (e.g. after bleeding or haemolysis).
White Blood Cells (Leukocytes)

Divided into granulocytes (polymorphonuclear: neutrophil, eosinophil, basophil) and agranulocytes (mononuclear: lymphocyte, monocyte).

🔬 Image slot — the five leukocytes for comparison (neutrophil, eosinophil, basophil, lymphocyte, monocyte)
Cell% of WBCsAppearanceMain role
Neutrophil40–75% (commonest)Multilobed nucleus (2–5 lobes); fine neutral/lilac granulesAcute bacterial infection; phagocytosis
Lymphocyte20–45%Large round dense nucleus; thin rim of pale-blue cytoplasmAdaptive immunity — B (antibodies), T (cell-mediated), NK
Monocyte2–10% (largest)Kidney/horseshoe nucleus; abundant grey-blue cytoplasmBecomes tissue macrophage/dendritic cell; phagocytosis & antigen presentation
Eosinophil1–6%Bilobed nucleus; large red-orange granulesParasites & allergy/type I hypersensitivity

Frequency mnemonic (commonest → rarest): Never Let Monkeys Eat Bananas — Neutrophils > Lymphocytes > Monocytes > Eosinophils > Basophils.
Left shift = more immature band neutrophils (acute infection). Hypersegmented neutrophils (>5 lobes) suggest B12/folate deficiency.
Platelets (Thrombocytes)
  • Not cells — anucleate cytoplasmic fragments shed from megakaryocytes
  • Small (~2–4 µm) purple granular bodies on the film
  • Haemostasis: adhere, activate and aggregate to form the platelet plug, and provide a phospholipid surface for the clotting cascade
  • Lifespan ~7–10 days
Haemopoiesis — Making Blood Cells

All blood cells arise from a pluripotent haematopoietic stem cell (HSC), which gives two lines:

Myeloid lineage
  • Erythrocytes, granulocytes (neutrophil/eosinophil/basophil), monocytes
  • Megakaryocytes → platelets
Lymphoid lineage
  • B, T and NK lymphocytes
Key maturation lines & their drivers
LineSequenceGrowth factor
ErythropoiesisProerythroblast → basophilic → polychromatic → orthochromatic erythroblast → extrudes nucleus → reticulocyte → RBCErythropoietin (EPO) from the kidney (hypoxia sensor)

Red vs yellow marrow: red marrow is active/haematopoietic; yellow marrow is fatty/inactive but can reconvert to red when demand rises (e.g. chronic haemolysis).
Stains & Sampling
  • Romanowsky stains (Giemsa / Wright / Leishman) — the standard for blood & marrow films
  • Supravital stain (new methylene blue) — reticulocytes
  • Perls' Prussian blue — iron stores in a marrow aspirate
  • Marrow is sampled as an aspirate (cytology) + trephine biopsy (architecture & cellularity)
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Anaemia
↓ Hb. Microcytic (iron def), macrocytic/megaloblastic (B12/folate — hypersegmented neutrophils), normocytic.
Abnormal RBC shapes
Sickle cells (sickle-cell disease), spherocytes (no central pallor), target cells.
Leukocytosis
Neutrophilia (bacterial), eosinophilia (parasite/allergy), lymphocytosis (viral), left shift.
Blasts on the film 🚨
Circulating blast cells suggest acute leukaemia — a haematological emergency.
Thrombocytopenia
Low platelets → bruising/bleeding; thrombocytosis → clotting risk.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Blood is a connective tissue with a liquid matrix (plasma); serum = plasma minus clotting factors.
RBC ~7–8 µm: anucleate biconcave disc with central pallor; lifespan 120 days; the on-film ruler.
WBC frequency: Never Let Monkeys Eat Bananas (Neutrophil > Lymphocyte > Monocyte > Eosinophil > Basophil).
Neutrophil = multilobed, bacterial infection; eosinophil = bilobed + red granules, parasites/allergy; basophil = dark granules hiding the nucleus.
Monocyte = largest WBC, horseshoe nucleus → tissue macrophage.
Platelets = megakaryocyte fragments (anucleate); reticulocytes = young RBCs (residual RNA, polychromasia).
Adult haemopoiesis = red bone marrow; fetal = liver/spleen; embryonic = yolk sac.
EPO (kidney) drives red cells; TPO drives platelets; G-CSF drives neutrophils.
Hypersegmented neutrophils → B12/folate deficiency; blasts on film → acute leukaemia.
BASIC TISSUES__Cartilage (hyaline, elast:
Overview — Cartilage as Specialised Connective Tissue

Cartilage is a firm-but-flexible specialised connective tissue — cells (chondrocytes) sit in an extensive, resilient extracellular matrix. Its defining quirk: it is avascular, aneural and alymphatic.

Avascular → nutrition by diffusion through the matrix. This is why cartilage heals slowly and poorly and tends to degenerate with age.
Matrix
  • Collagen — type II (hyaline & elastic); type I (fibrocartilage)
  • Ground substance — proteoglycans (aggrecan) + GAGs (chondroitin & keratan sulfate), highly hydrated
  • → the proteoglycan–water gel resists compression; collagen resists tension
Cells
  • Chondroblasts — secrete matrix at the surface
  • Chondrocytes — mature cells sitting in spaces called lacunae
  • Isogenous groups (cell nests) — clusters of chondrocytes from one dividing cell
Perichondrium = a dense connective-tissue sheath (outer fibrous + inner chondrogenic layer) covering most cartilage. It supplies nutrition and is the source of surface (appositional) growth. Exceptions with no perichondrium: articular hyaline cartilage and fibrocartilage.
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — hyaline cartilage: chondrocytes in lacunae, isogenous groups, perichondrium
  • Chondrocytes sitting in lacunae, often shrunken away from the lacuna wall (fixation artefact)
  • Isogenous groups (2–4 cells clustered together) — a give-away for cartilage
  • Basophilic (blue-purple) matrix — from the sulfated GAGs; darker territorial matrix rings each lacuna
  • A perichondrium at the edge (except articular/fibrocartilage)
The Three Types of Cartilage
🔬 Image slot — the three cartilage types side by side (hyaline / elastic / fibrocartilage)
HyalineElasticFibrocartilage
CollagenType II (masked, glassy)Type II + elastic fibresType I (thick, visible bundles)
PerichondriumYes (except articular)YesNo
Cellularity / lookGlassy homogeneous matrix; isogenous groupsDense network of elastic fibres in the matrixFew chondrocytes in rows between parallel collagen bundles
Main propertyResists compression; low frictionFlexible; recoils to shapeTensile strength + resists compression/shear
LocationsArticular surfaces, costal cartilage, trachea/bronchi, larynx, nose, epiphyseal growth plate, fetal skeletonExternal ear (pinna), epiglottis, auditory (Eustachian) tubeIntervertebral discs (annulus fibrosus), pubic symphysis, knee menisci, TMJ, some tendon/ligament insertions
The most common cartilage is hyaline — and it forms the fetal skeletal model and the epiphyseal growth plate (see the Bone note).
Structure → Function
Proteoglycan–water gel → resists compression (weight-bearing joints)
Type II collagen mesh → traps the gel & resists tension
Elastic fibres (elastic cartilage) → flexible recoil (the ear springs back)
Avascular → diffusion nutrition → slow, poor repair
How Cartilage Grows
Interstitial growth
  • Chondrocytes divide within the matrix (forming isogenous groups)
  • Growth from inside; young cartilage & the growth plate
Appositional growth
  • New cartilage added at the surface from the perichondrium
  • Growth from outside (adds width)
Stains & Ultrastructure
  • H&E — matrix is basophilic (sulfated GAGs); type II collagen is masked (same refractive index) so hyaline looks glassy
  • Toluidine blue / methylene blue — GAGs show metachromasia (purple)
  • Alcian blue & safranin O — stain proteoglycans (loss marks early osteoarthritis)
  • Elastic stain (Verhoeff / orcein) — confirms elastic cartilage
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Osteoarthritis
Progressive loss of articular hyaline cartilage (proteoglycan depletion) → joint pain; poor repair because avascular.
Disc herniation
Nucleus pulposus herniates through the fibrocartilage annulus fibrosus of the intervertebral disc.
Relapsing polychondritis
Autoimmune attack on cartilage → floppy/red ears, saddle-nose, airway collapse.
Achondroplasia
FGFR3 mutation disrupts the growth-plate (hyaline) → short-limb dwarfism.
Chondrosarcoma
Malignant tumour of cartilage-forming cells.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Cartilage is avascular — fed by diffusion, so it heals slowly.
Chondrocytes live in lacunae; clusters = isogenous groups (interstitial growth).
Hyaline & elastic = type II collagen; fibrocartilage = type I.
No perichondrium: fibrocartilage & articular cartilage.
Elastic cartilage → ear, epiglottis, auditory tube (needs to recoil).
Fibrocartilage → intervertebral discs, pubic symphysis, menisci (needs tensile strength).
Hyaline is the commonest and forms the fetal skeleton & growth plate.
Growth: interstitial (from within) vs appositional (from perichondrium).
GAGs give the matrix its basophilia and toluidine-blue metachromasia.
BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact, cancellous:
Overview — Bone as a Mineralised Connective Tissue

Bone is a specialised connective tissue whose defining feature is a calcified extracellular matrix — this is what makes it rigid, unlike every other connective tissue.

🔬 Image slot — long-bone structure / bone composition overview
Functions
Support & protection — skeleton, skull, thoracic cage
Movement — levers & muscle attachment
Mineral reservoir — ~99% of body calcium & phosphate; central to Ca²⁺ homeostasis
Haematopoiesis — houses red marrow
Endocrine — osteocalcin (metabolism), FGF23 (phosphate)
Matrix composition
Organic (~35%) — osteoid
  • Type I collagen (~90% of organic)
  • Ground substance: proteoglycans + glycoproteins (osteocalcin, osteonectin, osteopontin)
  • → tensile strength & flexibility
Inorganic (~65%) — mineral
  • Hydroxyapatite — Ca₁₀(PO₄)₆(OH)₂ crystals
  • Deposited on/along collagen fibrils
  • → compressive strength & hardness; mineral store
Reinforced-concrete analogy: collagen = the steel rods (resist stretching/tension); hydroxyapatite = the concrete (resists compression). Lose the mineral → rubbery bone (osteomalacia); lose/weaken the collagen → brittle bone (osteogenesis imperfecta).
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
  • Pink (eosinophilic) mineralised matrix in lamellae — parallel/concentric layers
  • Osteocytes sitting in lacunae (small dark spaces), linked by fine canaliculi
  • In compact bone: concentric lamellae around a central canal = an osteon (Haversian system) — the give-away
🔬 Image slot — compact bone osteon / Haversian system (ground section)
Ground section (undecalcified)
  • Cells are lost; lacunae & canaliculi fill with air/debris → appear black
  • Best for showing osteon architecture
Decalcified H&E
  • Mineral removed so tissue can be cut
  • Shows cells — osteocytes, surface osteoblasts, marrow
Bone must be decalcified (EDTA/acid) or ground thin before sectioning — the mineral is too hard for a microtome.
Compact vs Cancellous Bone
🔬 Image slot — compact (cortical) vs cancellous (trabecular) bone comparison
Compact (cortical)
  • Dense outer shell of the bone
  • Organised into osteons; central Haversian canal (longitudinal neurovascular channel)
  • Volkmann's (perforating) canals run transversely, connecting Haversian canals & periosteum
  • Interstitial lamellae (old osteon remnants) fill the gaps; circumferential lamellae at outer/inner surfaces
  • ~80% of skeletal mass; slow turnover
Cancellous (spongy / trabecular)
  • Network of trabeculae with marrow-filled spaces
  • No osteons — trabeculae are thin and nourished by diffusion from marrow
  • Trabeculae align along lines of stress (Wolff's law)
  • ~20% of mass but ~90% of surface area → metabolically active, high turnover (hit first in osteoporosis)
The Bone Cells
CellOriginRole & appearance
OsteoprogenitorMesenchymal stem cell (periosteum, endosteum)Divides & differentiates into osteoblasts
OsteoblastFrom osteoprogenitorBone-forming. Cuboidal, basophilic cytoplasm (abundant RER); secrete osteoid & initiate mineralisation; line bone surfaces
OsteocyteOsteoblast trapped in matrixMature cell in a lacuna; processes in canaliculi; maintain matrix & act as mechanosensors that direct remodelling
OsteoclastMonocyte/macrophage (haematopoietic) lineageBone-resorbing. Large, multinucleated; sit in Howship's lacunae; ruffled border secretes H⁺ (dissolves mineral) + cathepsin K (digests collagen)
🔬 Image slot — osteoclast in a Howship's lacuna & osteoblasts lining osteoid
RANK–RANKL–OPG axis: osteoblasts express RANKL, which binds RANK on osteoclast precursors → osteoclast formation & activation. OPG is a decoy receptor that blocks this. PTH & vitamin D raise RANKL → more resorption. (Denosumab is an anti-RANKL drug.)
Periosteum & Endosteum
Periosteum
  • Covers the external surface (except articular cartilage)
  • Outer fibrous layer + inner osteogenic (cambium) layer of osteoprogenitors
  • Anchored by Sharpey's fibres; richly vascular & sensory (pain)
Endosteum
  • Thin lining of internal surfaces — medullary cavity, Haversian canals, trabeculae
  • Osteoprogenitor + bone-lining cells
Bone Formation (Ossification)
Woven bone (immature)
  • Laid down rapidly; random collagen, more cells, weaker
  • Fetal skeleton, fracture callus, Paget's
Lamellar bone (mature)
  • Organised, parallel/concentric collagen; stronger
  • Progressively replaces woven bone
Two routes of formation
Intramembranous
  • Mesenchyme → osteoblasts → bone directly (no cartilage model)
  • Flat bones: skull vault, most facial bones, clavicle, mandible
Endochondral
  • Hyaline cartilage model is replaced by bone
  • Long bones, vertebrae, base of skull, most of the skeleton
  • Primary centre (diaphysis) + secondary centres (epiphyses)
🔬 Image slot — endochondral ossification & the epiphyseal growth-plate zones
Epiphyseal (growth) plate — 5 zones
1
Resting / reserveQuiescent hyaline cartilage; anchors the plate to the epiphysis
2
ProliferationChondrocytes divide and stack into columns → lengthening
3
HypertrophyChondrocytes enlarge
4
CalcificationCartilage matrix calcifies; chondrocytes die
5
OssificationOsteoblasts lay bone on the calcified cartilage spicules
The growth plate drives longitudinal growth and fuses after puberty (sex-steroid driven). Width of bone grows by appositional growth from the periosteum.
Bone Remodelling & Its Control

Bone is renewed lifelong by coupled resorption + formation at the Basic Multicellular Unit (BMU): osteoclasts resorb → reversal → osteoblasts form new osteoid → mineralisation. About 10% of the skeleton is replaced per year.

Repair microdamage
Adapt to load (Wolff's law)
Ca²⁺ homeostasis
Hormonal & mechanical control
FactorEffect on bone
PTH↑ resorption indirectly (osteoblast RANKL) → ↑ serum Ca²⁺. Intermittent low dose is anabolic (teriparatide)
Calcitriol (vit D)↑ gut Ca²⁺/PO₄ absorption → enables mineralisation; deficiency → osteomalacia/rickets
Calcitonin↓ osteoclast activity → ↓ serum Ca²⁺ (minor role in humans)
OestrogenRestrains resorption; menopausal loss → osteoporosis
Mechanical load↑ formation; immobility/microgravity → bone loss
Stains & Ultrastructure
  • Decalcified H&E — routine; shows cells & marrow
  • Ground section (undecalcified) — osteon detail; lacunae/canaliculi black
  • von Kossa — mineralised matrix black → distinguishes mineralised bone from unmineralised osteoid
  • Goldner's trichrome — mineralised bone green, osteoid red → diagnoses osteomalacia (wide red osteoid seams)
  • Tetracycline labelling — fluorescent; marks the mineralisation front to measure bone-formation rate
🔬 Image slot — von Kossa / Goldner's trichrome showing mineralised bone vs osteoid (optional)
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Osteoporosis
↓ bone mass, normal mineralisation; resorption > formation (age, menopause) → fragility fractures
Osteomalacia / Rickets
Defective mineralisation → excess unmineralised osteoid; vitamin D deficiency; soft bones
Paget's disease
Disordered, excessive remodelling; mosaic pattern of cement lines; enlarged weak bone
Osteogenesis imperfecta
Type I collagen defect → brittle bones, blue sclerae
Osteopetrosis
Osteoclast failure → dense but brittle bone, marrow crowding
Hyperparathyroidism
↑ resorption → osteitis fibrosa cystica, brown tumours
Fracture healing recapitulates development: haematoma → soft (fibrocartilaginous) callus → hard (woven-bone) callus → remodelling to lamellar bone.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Osteon (Haversian system) = structural unit of compact bone; cancellous bone has no osteons.
Osteoblast = basophilic, bone-forming; osteoclast = multinucleated, haematopoietic, resorbs in Howship's lacunae (cathepsin K + acid).
Only the osteoclast comes from the haematopoietic (monocyte) line — the rest are mesenchymal.
Volkmann's canals connect Haversian canals (transverse vs longitudinal).
Intramembranous = flat bones; endochondral = long bones (cartilage model).
Growth plate zones: Resting → Proliferation → Hypertrophy → Calcification → Ossification.
Osteoporosis = ↓ mass (normal mineralisation); osteomalacia = defective mineralisation (excess osteoid).
von Kossa blackens mineral; Goldner's separates mineralised bone (green) from osteoid (red).
Bone must be decalcified or ground before sectioning.
BASIC TISSUES__Muscle (skeletal, cardiac:
Overview — Muscle as a Contractile Tissue

Muscle is a tissue specialised for contraction — converting chemical energy (ATP) into mechanical force via the sliding of actin (thin) and myosin (thick) filaments. It is excitable, and (with the exception of some smooth muscle) is derived from mesoderm.

🔬 Image slot — the three muscle types side by side (skeletal, cardiac, smooth)
Shared vocabulary (the “sarco-” prefix)
Sarcolemma — the plasma membrane
Sarcoplasm — the cytoplasm
Sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) — smooth ER; stores & releases Ca²⁺
Myofibril — contractile rod of sarcomeres
Myofilaments — actin (thin) & myosin (thick)
Muscle fibre = a single muscle cell
All three types contract by the same core machinery (actin–myosin cross-bridges powered by ATP, triggered by a rise in cytosolic Ca²⁺). They differ in how the cells are arranged, how Ca²⁺ couples to contraction, and how they are controlled.
How to Recognise Each Type on a Slide ⭐

Ask three questions in order: (1) striations? (2) how many nuclei & where? (3) branched or not?

🔬 Image slot — skeletal (peripheral nuclei, striations) vs cardiac (central nucleus, intercalated discs) vs smooth (spindle nuclei)
Skeletal
  • Cross-striations present
  • Long, cylindrical, unbranched fibres
  • Multinucleated, nuclei pushed to the periphery (just under the sarcolemma)
Cardiac
  • Cross-striations present (fainter)
  • Branched fibres
  • 1–2 central nuclei
  • Intercalated discs — dark transverse lines (the give-away)
Smooth
  • No striations (uniform pink)
  • Fusiform (spindle-shaped) cells
  • Single central nucleus, “cigar-” shaped (corkscrews when contracted)
Fast discriminators: peripheral nuclei + big fibres → skeletal; central nucleus + branching + intercalated discs → cardiac; no striations + spindle nuclei → smooth.
The Three Types Compared
FeatureSkeletalCardiacSmooth
Cell shapeLong cylindrical, unbranchedBranchedFusiform / spindle
NucleiMany, peripheral1–2, central1, central
StriationsYesYesNo
Intercalated discsNoYesNo
ControlVoluntary (somatic)Involuntary (autonomic + intrinsic)Involuntary (autonomic, hormones, stretch)
Ca²⁺ sensorTroponin CTroponin CCalmodulin → MLCK
T-tubule systemTriad (at A–I junction)Diad (at Z line)None (caveolae instead)
Pacemaker / gap junctionsNoYes (functional syncytium)Yes (single-unit type)
RegenerationLimited — satellite cellsVery poor (scar forms)Good (cells re-enter mitosis)
Example locationAttached to skeleton, tongue, diaphragmHeart wall (myocardium)Gut, vessels, airways, uterus, iris
Skeletal Muscle — Organisation
Connective-tissue wrappings (outside → in)
1
EpimysiumDense CT around the whole muscle
2
PerimysiumWraps a fascicle (bundle of fibres); carries larger vessels & nerves
3
EndomysiumDelicate reticular CT around each fibre; capillaries & satellite cells
🔬 Image slot — skeletal muscle cross-section showing epimysium / perimysium / endomysium and fascicles
Fibre → myofibril → sarcomere

Each fibre is packed with myofibrils; the myofibril is a chain of sarcomeres — the functional/contractile unit, running Z line to Z line. The register of sarcomeres across adjacent myofibrils produces the visible cross-striations.

🔬 Image slot — sarcomere ultrastructure — A band, I band, Z line, H zone, M line; thick & thin filaments
Band / lineWhat it isBehaviour on contraction
A bandFull length of thick (myosin) filaments (dark, anisotropic)Unchanged
I bandThin (actin) only (light, isotropic); bisected by the Z lineShortens
H zoneThick only (no overlap), centre of A bandShortens
Z line (disc)Anchors thin filaments; sarcomere boundary (α-actinin)Z lines move closer
M lineAnchors thick filaments at the centreUnchanged
Sliding-filament theory: the filaments don’t shorten — they slide past each other, so the I band and H zone narrow while the A band stays constant. Ca²⁺ binds troponin C → tropomyosin shifts → myosin heads engage actin → ATP-powered power stroke.
Excitation–contraction coupling — the triad
Triad
  • One T-tubule + two terminal cisternae of SR
  • Located at the A–I junction (two triads per sarcomere)
  • Depolarisation travels down the T-tubule → SR releases Ca²⁺
Satellite cells
  • Quiescent myogenic stem cells between sarcolemma & basal lamina
  • Activate to repair / regenerate fibres (limited capacity)
Cardiac Muscle — the Intercalated Disc
🔬 Image slot — cardiac muscle — branching striated fibres, central nuclei, dark intercalated discs
  • Branched, striated cells with 1–2 central nuclei; abundant mitochondria (high aerobic demand) and lipofuscin (wear-and-tear pigment) with age.
  • Cells join end-to-end at intercalated discs — the defining feature, made of three junctions:
Fascia adherens — anchors thin filaments (like a Z line); transmits force cell-to-cell
Desmosomes (maculae adherentes) — mechanical anchoring; stop cells pulling apart
Gap junctions — electrical coupling → functional syncytium
EC coupling
  • Diad: one T-tubule + one SR cisterna, at the Z line (T-tubules larger than skeletal)
  • Ca²⁺-induced Ca²⁺ release — extracellular Ca²⁺ entry triggers SR release
Regeneration
  • No satellite cells → virtually no regeneration
  • Injury (MI) heals by fibrous scar, not new muscle
Purkinje fibres are modified cardiac myocytes: larger, pale (glycogen-rich), few myofibrils — specialised for rapid conduction, not contraction (see the Cardiac Conducting System note).
Smooth Muscle — No Sarcomeres
🔬 Image slot — smooth muscle — interlacing sheets of spindle cells with central cigar-shaped nuclei
  • Fusiform cells, single central nucleus; actin & myosin present but not in ordered sarcomeres → no striations.
  • Thin filaments anchor to dense bodies (cytoplasmic, contain α-actinin — the Z-line equivalent) and dense plaques on the membrane.
  • Caveolae (surface invaginations) substitute for T-tubules; sparse SR.
  • Contraction is Ca²⁺–calmodulin → myosin light-chain kinase (MLCK) — there is no troponin. Slow, sustained, energy-efficient (“latch” state).
Single-unit (visceral)
  • Coupled by gap junctions → contract as a sheet
  • Often spontaneously active (pacemaker); gut, ureter, uterus, small vessels
Multi-unit
  • Each cell individually innervated, few gap junctions → fine graded control
  • Iris, ciliary body, vas deferens, large arteries
Smooth muscle synthesises its own matrix (collagen, elastin, proteoglycans) and retains the ability to divide — key in vascular remodelling and uterine hypertrophy in pregnancy.
Innervation & the Neuromuscular Junction
🔬 Image slot — neuromuscular junction / motor end plate (optional)
Skeletal — motor end plate
  • A motor neuron + all the fibres it supplies = a motor unit
  • Nerve terminal releases ACh → nicotinic receptors on the junctional folds → end-plate potential
  • ACh broken down by acetylcholinesterase
Cardiac & smooth — autonomic
  • No discrete end plate; varicosities (“boutons en passant”) release transmitter over a wide area
  • Sympathetic (noradrenaline) & parasympathetic (ACh, muscarinic) modulate intrinsic activity
Fibre typing (skeletal): Type I = slow, oxidative, red (myoglobin/mitochondria rich, fatigue-resistant — postural muscles); Type II = fast, glycolytic, pale (rapid powerful bursts, fatigue quickly). Demonstrated with myosin ATPase histochemistry.
Stains & Markers
  • H&E — routine; striations & intercalated discs visible; nuclear position separates the types
  • PTAH (phosphotungstic acid haematoxylin) — classic stain for cross-striations and intercalated discs (blue)
  • Masson trichrome — muscle red, collagen blue/green → shows fibrosis (e.g. post-MI scar, dystrophy)
  • PAS — glycogen (abundant in muscle & Purkinje fibres)
  • Myosin ATPase — distinguishes Type I vs Type II fibres
  • Immunohistochemistry — desmin (all muscle), myoglobin/MyoD/myogenin (skeletal, rhabdomyosarcoma), α-smooth-muscle actin (SMA) & desmin (smooth muscle/leiomyoma), dystrophin (absent in Duchenne)
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Duchenne / Becker dystrophy
Dystrophin gene defect → fibre necrosis, variation in fibre size, fatty/fibrous replacement; absent dystrophin on IHC
Myasthenia gravis
Autoantibodies vs nicotinic ACh receptor at the NMJ → fatigable weakness
Myocardial infarction
Cardiac myocytes can’t regenerate → healing by collagenous scar; surviving myocytes hypertrophy
Denervation atrophy
Loss of nerve supply → angular atrophic fibres, fibre-type grouping on reinnervation
Leiomyoma / leiomyosarcoma
Smooth-muscle tumours (uterine fibroid = benign leiomyoma); SMA/desmin positive
Rhabdomyosarcoma
Malignant skeletal-muscle tumour of children; desmin/myogenin positive
Hypertrophy vs hyperplasia: skeletal & cardiac muscle enlarge only by hypertrophy (bigger cells — e.g. LV in hypertension); smooth muscle can do both hypertrophy and hyperplasia (e.g. the pregnant uterus).
⭐ Exam Pearls
Peripheral, multiple nuclei = skeletal; central + intercalated discs = cardiac; no striations + spindle nucleus = smooth.
Intercalated discs = fascia adherens + desmosomes + gap junctions (electrical coupling → syncytium). Only in cardiac.
Sarcomere = Z line to Z line. On contraction the I band & H zone shorten; the A band does not.
A band = myosin (dark); I band = actin only (light). Mnemonic: myA= A band myosin; aI= actin thI n / I band.
Skeletal = triad at A–I junction (2 SR cisternae); cardiac = diad at Z line (1 cisterna); smooth = caveolae, no T-tubules.
Ca²⁺ sensor: troponin (skeletal & cardiac) vs calmodulin–MLCK (smooth — no troponin).
Regeneration: smooth > skeletal (satellite cells) > cardiac (none → scar).
Type I = slow/oxidative/red (postural); Type II = fast/glycolytic/pale (bursts).
Wrappings outer→inner: Epimysium (muscle) → Perimysium (fascicle) → Endomysium (fibre).
Desmin marks all muscle; SMA = smooth; dystrophin absent in Duchenne.
BASIC TISSUES__Nervous Tissue (neurons,:
Overview — Nervous Tissue

Nervous tissue is specialised for rapid communication — sensing, integrating and signalling. It is built from just two cell classes:

Neurons
  • The excitable, signalling cells
  • Generate & conduct action potentials; communicate at synapses
  • Post-mitotic (mostly cannot divide)
Neuroglia (glia)
  • The supporting cells — ~10× more numerous
  • Insulation (myelin), metabolic & structural support, immune defence, ionic buffering
  • Retain the ability to divide (source of most primary brain tumours)
🔬 Image slot — neuron + surrounding glia; grey matter vs white matter overview
Origins: neurons & most glia arise from neuroectoderm (neural tube = CNS; neural crest = PNS neurons, Schwann & satellite cells). Microglia are the exception — they come from mesoderm (monocyte lineage).
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — grey matter (neuron cell bodies + neuropil) vs white matter (myelinated tracts)
  • Neuron cell body — large, with a pale (euchromatic) nucleus and a single prominent nucleolus (“owl-eye”), surrounded by basophilic Nissl substance.
  • Neuropil — the pink felt-like background of interwoven dendrites, axons & glial processes (between cell bodies in grey matter).
  • Glia — only their small nuclei are usually visible on H&E; the cytoplasm & processes need special stains.
Grey matter
  • Neuron cell bodies, dendrites, synapses & glia
  • Cortex & deep nuclei (CNS); outside in brain, inside (H-shape) in cord
White matter
  • Myelinated axon tracts + glia; few/no cell bodies
  • Pale because of lipid-rich myelin
The Neuron
🔬 Image slot — multipolar neuron — soma with Nissl bodies, dendrites, axon hillock, axon
PartFeatures
Cell body (soma / perikaryon)Metabolic centre; large euchromatic nucleus + prominent nucleolus; Nissl bodies (RER + free ribosomes) → basophilic
DendritesReceptive processes; multiple, tapering, branched; contain Nissl; often bear spines
Axon hillockCone of origin of the axon; lacks Nissl; site of action-potential initiation (initial segment)
AxonSingle, uniform-calibre; conducts away from the soma; no Nissl; relies on axonal transport
Axon terminal (bouton)Forms the presynaptic element; contains synaptic vesicles & mitochondria
Axonal transport: anterograde (kinesin, soma→terminal) delivers organelles/vesicles; retrograde (dynein, terminal→soma) recycles & carries signals — also the route for rabies & tetanus toxin and herpes.
Classification by number of processes
Multipolar — 1 axon + many dendrites; commonest (motor neurons, interneurons)
Bipolar — 1 axon + 1 dendrite (retina, olfactory, vestibulocochlear)
Pseudounipolar — single process that splits; dorsal root ganglion sensory neurons
Unipolar — one process (mainly invertebrates / some embryonic)
By function
  • Sensory (afferent) — toward CNS · Motor (efferent) — away from CNS · Interneurons — connect the two (majority of CNS neurons)
Neuroglia — the Supporting Cast
🔬 Image slot — the glial cell types — astrocyte, oligodendrocyte, microglia, ependyma, Schwann cell
Glial cellLocationFunction & marker
AstrocyteCNSMost abundant glia; structural/metabolic support, K⁺ & neurotransmitter buffering, form the blood–brain barrier via end-feet, and the glial scar. Marker GFAP. Fibrous (white matter) vs protoplasmic (grey matter)
OligodendrocyteCNSMyelinates CNS axons — one cell wraps several axons
MicrogliaCNSResident macrophages (mesodermal/monocyte origin); immune surveillance & phagocytosis
Ependymal cellsCNSCiliated cuboidal/columnar lining of ventricles & central canal; circulate CSF; specialised as choroid plexus (CSF production)
Schwann cellPNSMyelinates PNS axons — one cell = one internode; also ensheaths unmyelinated axons. Marker S100
Satellite cellPNSSurround neuron cell bodies in ganglia; regulate microenvironment
Myelin, one cell, how many axons? Oligodendrocyte = many CNS axons; Schwann cell = one PNS internode. This is why one oligodendrocyte lesion can hit several tracts (MS).
Myelin, Nodes of Ranvier & Conduction
🔬 Image slot — myelinated fibre — internodes, node of Ranvier, Schwann cell / oligodendrocyte wrapping
  • Myelin = concentric wraps of glial plasma membrane → a lipid-rich insulator; appears as a clear halo on H&E (lipid dissolved in processing), stained by Luxol fast blue / osmium.
  • Nodes of Ranvier — periodic gaps in myelin, packed with voltage-gated Na⁺ channels.
  • Saltatory conduction — the impulse “jumps” node-to-node → faster & more efficient than unmyelinated conduction.
CNS myelin
  • Oligodendrocyte; one cell → up to ~50 axons
  • No neurilemma, no basal lamina → poor regeneration
PNS myelin
  • Schwann cell; one cell = one internode
  • Neurilemma (Schwann cytoplasm + basal lamina) → guides regeneration
Peripheral Nerve Organisation
🔬 Image slot — peripheral nerve cross-section — endoneurium, perineurium, epineurium, fascicles
1
EndoneuriumDelicate CT around each axon + its Schwann sheath
2
PerineuriumWraps a fascicle; specialised epithelioid cells form the blood–nerve barrier
3
EpineuriumDense CT around the whole nerve; carries the vasa nervorum
Same nested plan as skeletal muscle (endo–peri–epi). The perineurium is the immunological barrier of peripheral nerve.
Ganglia
Dorsal root (sensory) ganglion
  • Pseudounipolar cell bodies in ordered rows, ringed by satellite cells
Autonomic ganglion
  • Multipolar cell bodies, scattered; eccentric nuclei
The Synapse
🔬 Image slot — chemical synapse (EM) — presynaptic vesicles, cleft, postsynaptic density (optional)
Chemical synapse
  • Presynaptic terminal with neurotransmitter vesicles + mitochondria
  • Synaptic cleft (~20–40 nm)
  • Postsynaptic density bearing receptors
  • Ca²⁺ entry → vesicle fusion → transmitter release — unidirectional
Electrical synapse
  • Gap junctions — direct ionic flow
  • Very fast, bidirectional; synchronises groups of cells
Synapse types by site: axo-dendritic (commonest), axo-somatic, axo-axonic. Synaptophysin is the standard IHC marker of synaptic vesicles.
Stains & Markers
  • H&E — Nissl substance basophilic; myelin appears as clear halos
  • Nissl stain (cresyl violet / toluidine blue) — stains Nissl → highlights cell bodies, used to map grey matter
  • Silver stains (Golgi, Bielschowsky) — blacken neurofibrils / axons & dendrites; Bielschowsky shows Alzheimer plaques & tangles
  • Luxol fast blue — stains myelin blue (with PAS/cresyl violet counterstain)
  • Osmium tetroxide — blackens myelin lipid (EM & teased-fibre preparations)
  • Immunohistochemistry — GFAP (astrocytes), S100 (Schwann/melanocytes), NeuN (neuronal nuclei), synaptophysin (synapses), neurofilament (axons)
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Multiple sclerosis
CNS demyelination (oligodendrocyte target) → plaques; loss of Luxol staining
Guillain–Barré syndrome
PNS demyelination (Schwann/root target) → ascending weakness
Gliosis (astrocytosis)
Reactive astrocytes proliferate → glial scar (the CNS equivalent of a fibrous scar)
Wallerian degeneration
Distal axon degenerates after transection; PNS regenerates (Schwann/neurilemma guide); CNS does not
Chromatolysis
Axon injury → Nissl disperses, nucleus moves to periphery, soma swells — a repair response
Gliomas
Tumours of glia (e.g. astrocytoma/glioblastoma, GFAP⁺); neurons rarely form tumours
Alzheimer’s disease
Neurofibrillary tangles (tau) & amyloid plaques — shown on silver stains
Parkinson’s disease
Loss of substantia-nigra neurons + cytoplasmic Lewy bodies (α-synuclein)
⭐ Exam Pearls
Nissl substance (RER) is in the soma & dendrites but NOT the axon or axon hillock.
Neuron nucleus = large, pale, single prominent nucleolus (“owl-eye”).
CNS myelin = oligodendrocyte (many axons); PNS myelin = Schwann cell (one internode).
Microglia are the odd ones out — mesodermal (monocyte) origin; all other glia are neuroectodermal.
Astrocytes = BBB end-feet, K⁺ buffering, glial scar; marker GFAP. Schwann/satellite marker S100.
Saltatory conduction jumps node-to-node (Na⁺ channels at nodes of Ranvier).
Nerve wrappings: Endoneurium (axon) → Perineurium (fascicle, blood–nerve barrier) → Epineurium (whole nerve).
PNS regenerates (neurilemma guides); CNS does not (glial scar, no neurilemma).
Dorsal root ganglion = pseudounipolar cells + satellite cells in rows; MS = CNS, GBS = PNS demyelination.
Chemical synapse is unidirectional; synaptophysin marks vesicles.
